title: CNAS Insights | Japan isn’t rearming. It’s adapting to a new era.
gist: The correct frame for Japan's defense shift is not rearmament but the systematic removal of self-imposed constraints - Japan spent a higher share of GDP on defense in the 1950s and had nearly twice today's tank count in the early 1990s. What is new is long-range strike, de facto carriers, a joint command, a first centralized intelligence agency since 1945, relaxed lethal-export rules, and Patriot manufacturing sold back to the United States - all driven as much by doubt about American reliability as by China.

insights.claim: Japan is undergoing a defense revolution but not a rearmament, because what matters more than added capability is the systematic elimination of self-imposed constraints that hobbled Japanese defense for decades.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Reframes Japan's shift as an irreversible institutional unlock rather than a budget cycle - implies durable multi-decade demand for Japanese defense capability and exports.
insights.quote: While it is growing stronger, more important than the additions are what is being removed. Tokyo is systematically eliminating the self-imposed constraints that hobbled Japanese defense for decades.
insights.locator: Japan is indeed undergoing a defense revolution

insights.claim: Japan spent a higher percentage of GDP on defense in the 1950s than it does today, and by 1989 briefly had the world's third-largest defense budget, contradicting claims that Japan was previously unarmed.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Historical baseline shows current spending is a recovery, not a break - the ceiling on Japanese defense spending is higher than most assume.
insights.quote: Tokyo spent, for example, a higher percentage of its GDP on defense in the 1950s than it does today. By 1989, largely as a result of the strong yen, Japan briefly had the world’s third-largest defense budget.

insights.claim: In the early 1990s Japan's ground Self-Defense Forces were about a fifth larger than today and once fielded nearly twice as many tanks, meaning the force has shrunk in mass even as it modernizes.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Modernization is qualitative, not a manpower or armor build-out - spending will concentrate in missiles, ships, ISR and enablers rather than land platforms.
insights.quote:
In the early 1990s, the ground SDF was about a fifth larger than it is
today, and it once had nearly twice the number of tanks it now possesses.

insights.claim: The specific postwar constraints being lifted were the bans on collective self-defense, on lethal weapons export, on long-range strike capability, and the absence of a joint command - each an identifiable policy lock rather than a capability gap.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A checklist of removed constraints gives a concrete scorecard for how far the transformation has run and what remains (constitutional revision).
insights.quote: It could not engage in collective self-defense, banned the export of lethal weapons, did not possess the ability to strike long-range targets in foreign countries, and lacked a joint command.

insights.claim: Chinese and Russian officials frame Japan's shift as resurgent militarism, with Foreign Minister Wang Yi calling to prevent the resurgence of Japanese militarism and Moscow urging Tokyo to make a clean break with militarism.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Expect continued Chinese and Russian rhetorical and economic pressure on Japan, which can translate into targeted trade coercion against Japanese firms.
insights.quote: resolutely prevent the resurgence of Japanese militarism.
insights.locator: To some, these advances amount to rearmament

insights.claim: Japan has bought Tomahawk missiles enabling strikes on targets more than 1,000 kilometres away, its first genuine long-range strike capability.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Long-range strike changes the regional targeting calculus and creates recurring Japanese demand for US and domestic missile inventory.
insights.quote: Japan has bought long-range strike weapons, including Tomahawk missiles that allow it to hit targets more than 1,000 kilometers away.

insights.claim: Two modified Japanese destroyers now function effectively as aircraft carriers with F-35s able to fly from them - Japan's first carriers since 1945.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Carrier-capable Japan extends allied air power in the western Pacific and locks in F-35B-class procurement and sustainment demand.
insights.quote: Two modified destroyers today function effectively as aircraft carriers, Japan’s first since 1945.

insights.claim: Japan is developing a hypersonic glide vehicle, jointly developing a sixth-generation fighter, and seeking nuclear-propelled submarines.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A programme pipeline spanning hypersonics, next-gen air and nuclear propulsion means sustained high-end R&D budgets and partner opportunities for allied primes.
insights.quote: Japan is developing a hypersonic glide vehicle, working on joint development of a sixth-generation fighter, and seeks nuclear-propelled submarines.

insights.claim: With global demand for missile interceptors vastly outstripping supply, Japan is manufacturing Patriots and selling them to the United States - reversing the traditional direction of alliance arms flows.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Japan is becoming a supply node in the US munitions base, not just a customer - a structural change in allied defense-industrial trade worth tracking for Japanese primes.
insights.quote: As global demand for missile interceptors vastly outstrips supply, Japan is manufacturing Patriots—and selling them to the United States.

insights.claim: Japan relaxed its longstanding ban on lethal weapons exports in April and has already sealed a multibillion-dollar deal to sell warships to Australia.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Japan entering the global arms export market adds a credible new competitor in naval platforms and a growth vector for Japanese shipbuilders.
insights.quote: In April, Japan relaxed its longstanding ban on the export of lethal weapons and has sealed a multibillion-dollar deal to sell warships to Australia.

insights.claim: Japan established a new Joint Operations Command last year to allow quicker and more effective decision-making and planning, ending decades without a joint command.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Command integration is the precondition for combined operations with US forces - it materially raises the credibility of allied deterrence in a Taiwan contingency.
insights.quote: Japan last year established a new Joint Operations Command that will allow for quicker, more effective decision-making and planning.

insights.claim: Japan's newly announced National Intelligence Bureau is the country's first centralized intelligence agency since 1945.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Centralized intelligence reduces Japanese dependence on US intelligence and creates new demand for cyber and information-security capability.
insights.quote: Its newly announced National Intelligence Bureau represents the first centralized intelligence agency in Japan since 1945.

insights.claim: Japan will rewrite and reissue three key strategic documents - the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy and the Defense Buildup Program - by the end of this year.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A dated policy catalyst: the reissued Buildup Program will set the multi-year procurement envelope Japanese and allied suppliers bid against.
insights.quote: by the end of this year, three key strategic documents—the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program—will be rewritten and reissued

insights.claim: Takaichi in May called for a debate on revising Japan's constitution so that it is updated to reflect the demands of the times, the most ambitious of the current constraint removals.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Constitutional revision is the final lock; movement on it would signal that the defense transformation is permanent rather than administration-specific.
insights.quote: Takaichi in May called for a debate on revising the Japanese constitution, ensuring that it is “updated to reflect the demands of the times.”

insights.claim: Japan and the United States have begun a dialogue on extended nuclear deterrence, a subject historically avoided in the alliance.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Opening the nuclear-umbrella conversation is a marker of Japanese doubt about US guarantees and a precursor to harder debates in Tokyo and Seoul.
insights.quote: Japan and the United States have begun a dialogue on extended nuclear deterrence.

insights.claim: Takaichi pledged to hit the 2 percent of GDP defense spending target two years early, with Japan just under that figure at the end of 2026 and further increases being sketched out.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Acceleration past the prior target with new increments already drafted means Japanese defense budget growth is not yet at its peak.
insights.quote: Takaichi pledged to hit the previous target—spending 2 percent of GDP on defense—two years early. Japan will be just under this figure at the end of 2026 and is sketching out future increases.

insights.claim: Japan has become the world's tenth-biggest defense spender.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A top-ten defense budget makes Japan a market large enough to sustain a domestic prime ecosystem and to matter to global suppliers.
insights.quote:
Today, Japan has become the world’s tenth-biggest
defense spender.

insights.claim: Japan carries the highest debt-to-GDP ratio of any advanced economy and has an aging population, so there will be inevitable limits to how far defense spending can rise.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The fiscal and demographic ceiling caps the Japanese defense trade - prioritization fights between exquisite programmes and mass are coming.
insights.quote: Japan carries the highest debt-to-GDP ratio of any advanced economy and has an aging population; there will be inevitable limits to its defense spending.

insights.claim: Washington should help Tokyo buy wisely by questioning whether expensive projects like nuclear-propelled submarines are necessary and whether a sixth-generation fighter is realistic.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Flags the two Japanese programmes most at risk of cancellation or descoping under fiscal pressure.
insights.quote: Washington can help Tokyo buy wisely, thinking hard about whether expensive projects like nuclear-propelled submarines are necessary and whether developing a sixth-generation fighter is realistic.

insights.claim: A poll last year showed more than 75 percent of Japanese did not believe the United States would defend their country, a striking erosion of confidence in the sole ally guaranteeing Japanese security.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Public disbelief in the US guarantee is the political fuel for autonomous Japanese capability - it makes the buildout resilient to changes in Washington.
insights.quote: A poll last year showed that more than 75 percent of Japanese did not believe the United States would defend their country.
insights.locator: The Trump administration has had an inconsistent approach

insights.claim: Japan's military build-up serves two purposes at once: demonstrating alliance value to keep America committed, and hedging against both regional threats and US inconstancy.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Dual-purpose logic means Japanese spending rises whether US commitment strengthens or weakens - an unusually robust demand signal.
insights.quote: Japanese leaders seek to demonstrate their value to the alliance, helping assure America’s continued commitment. But a stronger military also helps Japan hedge, both against the region’s rising threats and the possibility of U.S. inconstancy.
insights.locator: Tokyo’s pursuit of a more powerful

insights.claim: The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Japan and demanded higher defense spending and clarity on a Taiwan contingency, then stayed largely silent when China retaliated against Takaichi with punitive measures for complying.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Allies that take political risk for Washington and are not backed will hedge harder - watch for Japanese diversification of security and trade partners.
insights.quote: After Takaichi publicly did so, China retaliated with a raft of punitive measures that elicited mostly silence from Washington.
insights.locator: The Trump administration has had an inconsistent approach

insights.claim: Japan wants US attention and resources focused on the Indo-Pacific but watches another costly and inconclusive Middle East war absorb Washington's bandwidth.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The Middle East war is a direct opportunity cost against Indo-Pacific deterrence - a variable Asian allies are explicitly pricing.
insights.quote: Japan strives to focus American attention and resources on the Indo-Pacific but watches as yet another costly and inconclusive war in the Middle East absorbs Washington’s attention.
insights.locator: The Trump administration has had an inconsistent approach

insights.claim: Takaichi's moment of domestic political dominance has freed the Liberal Democratic Party to unshackle defense policy quickly, making the current window unusually productive for reform.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The pace of Japanese reform is tied to one leader's political capital - a domestic political reversal is the main risk to the transformation timeline.
insights.quote: Takaichi’s moment of domestic political dominance has freed the Liberal Democratic Party to unshackle its defense policy.
insights.locator: Tokyo’s pursuit of a more powerful

insights.claim: Japan's 2022 National Defense Strategy declared the most severe and complex security environment since the end of WWII and called for fundamentally reinforcing defense capabilities, marking the formal turn in policy.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The 2022 document is the origin point of the current cycle; the end-2026 rewrite will show how much further the threat assessment has moved.
insights.quote: Amid the most severe and complex security environment since the end of WWII,

insights.claim: The stimulus is China's combination of growing power projection and aggressive foreign policy - pressuring Taiwan, patrolling the Senkakus, economic coercion, South China Sea militarization and gray-zone activity in the western Pacific.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Enumerates the specific Chinese behaviors that will keep Japanese threat perception elevated regardless of any diplomatic thaw.
insights.quote: including pressuring Taiwan, patrolling the Senkaku Islands, employing economic coercion, militarizing the South China Sea, and engaging in gray-zone activities in the western Pacific

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine alarmed Japanese planners by demonstrating that forcible conquest and annexation of sovereign territory is again possible - in Europe now, potentially in Asia later.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Ukraine is the demonstration effect underwriting Asian defense budgets - the Europe-to-Asia read-across is explicit in Japanese planning.
insights.quote: Suddenly the unthinkable—the forcible conquest and annexation of sovereign territory—was possible, then in Europe but perhaps tomorrow in Asia.

insights.claim: Washington can aid the allied defense industrial base by buying Japanese, especially in ships and munitions, turning Japan into a source of allied production capacity.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: US procurement of Japanese ships and munitions would be a direct revenue channel for Japanese heavy industry and a partial fix for US shipbuilding shortfalls.
insights.quote: It can aid the defense industrial base by buying Japanese, especially in ships and munitions.
